articles.title: Planning how to find pantry supplies during a power cut
articles.summary: Keep food locations legible when fixed lighting is unavailable.

visual.alt: A compact sequence diagram labels Locate, Light, Check to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Map storage before an outage
paragraphs: Walk through the usual food storage areas in normal lighting and note which shelves, drawers and cupboards are difficult to distinguish without overhead lights.
Keep a simple written or offline location list, so household members can find essential supplies without searching unfamiliar spaces in the dark.

sections.title: Choose safer ways to see contents
paragraphs: Identify a working battery-powered light and a convenient storage position that can be reached without crossing cluttered areas.
Avoid open flames as cupboard lighting and do not place portable lights where they obstruct access, fall into water or create other avoidable hazards.

sections.title: Practise a calm retrieval
paragraphs: Try locating a common food item using the chosen portable light during an ordinary household check, without deliberately creating an unsafe blackout.
If the route is awkward, improve the storage arrangement rather than relying on memory. Update the list when cupboards or household needs change.

articles.title: Keeping a register of household water containers
articles.summary: Distinguish containers intended for drinking water from other household uses.

visual.alt: A compact checklist diagram labels Purpose, Location, Condition to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Record what each container is for
paragraphs: List reusable bottles, jugs and other household containers by their normal purpose and storage location. Distinguish containers intended for drinking water from those used for cleaning or other tasks.
Do not infer that an unlabelled container or a container used for non-food substances is suitable for drinking water. Material suitability and manufacturer instructions matter.

sections.title: Keep identifying details visible
paragraphs: Record container type, lid condition and any original product or care instructions in the inventory. Where a container is shared, use plain labels that remain legible after normal handling.
Avoid putting potentially misleading claims such as sterile or purified on a container merely because it has been cleaned. A label is an identification aid, not proof of water quality.

sections.title: Review before relying on it
paragraphs: During a normal supply check, note containers with missing caps, unclear purpose, damage or uncertain history and keep them separate from drinking-water equipment.
Water quality and treatment decisions require reliable current guidance and appropriate expert review. This article only organises household container records.

articles.title: Recording household food preferences without rigid rationing
articles.summary: Document preferences and access needs so supplies are practical for everyone.

visual.alt: A compact checklist diagram labels Ask, Record, Revisit to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Ask about practical needs
paragraphs: Invite household members to describe foods they normally eat, avoid or cannot use, without pressuring them to disclose medical information to other household members.
Separate ordinary preferences from important restrictions that may affect whether a proposed food item is suitable. Avoid treating one person's preferred food as universally appropriate.

sections.title: Make the record useful
paragraphs: Use a short private household note to record preferred staple categories, preparation limitations and who should be consulted before shared supplies are changed.
Include the location of suitable alternatives where the household already has them. Do not turn this into a fixed ration or a substitute for individual nutrition advice.

sections.title: Revisit as circumstances change
paragraphs: Review the note when household membership, food access or equipment changes. Ask before replacing familiar supplies with unfamiliar products.
Keep the information accessible to authorised household members only. The goal is fewer unsuitable purchases and less confusion during a disruption.

articles.title: Reconciling pantry purchases with what arrived
articles.summary: Use a simple receipt check to avoid counting missing or substituted food.

visual.alt: A compact sequence diagram labels Compare, Inspect, Update to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Compare the order with actual items
paragraphs: After a delivery or shop, compare the order or receipt with what physically arrived, paying attention to missing items, replacements and quantities.
A paid receipt does not confirm that every item is present. Avoid adding ordered quantities to the pantry inventory before checking the delivered goods.

sections.title: Check substitutions separately
paragraphs: If a different brand or size was supplied, record its actual product name and amount rather than assuming it matches the original order.
Read the substituted item's own allergen and storage information where relevant. Similar packaging and product names are not evidence that ingredients or handling requirements are identical.

sections.title: Update the household record
paragraphs: Adjust stock counts only after the items have been put away in their real locations. Keep a brief note of unresolved missing or damaged items for follow-up with the seller.
Discard temporary receipt notes when no longer needed, especially if they include payment or address information that does not belong in a shared inventory.

articles.title: Setting sensible reorder reminders for kitchen essentials
articles.summary: Create practical restocking prompts without pretending a stock threshold fits every household.

visual.alt: A compact sequence diagram labels Notice, Confirm, Restock to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Choose items worth tracking
paragraphs: Identify supplies whose absence would disrupt normal food preparation or household cleaning, such as washing-up materials, bin liners and commonly used shelf-stable ingredients.
Use ordinary household experience to decide which items need reminders. A single universal minimum quantity would ignore different household sizes, routines and storage space.

sections.title: Separate reminders from real stock
paragraphs: Create a reminder when supplies appear low, but mark it as a prompt rather than proof that a replacement has been purchased.
Check the physical storage area before placing an order. An app count can be out of date when someone uses, moves or shares an item without recording it.

sections.title: Close the loop
paragraphs: After restocking, record what actually arrived and where it was placed. Remove or defer reminders for items that are no longer needed.
Review reminder usefulness periodically; frequent false alerts make the system harder to trust during an actual disruption.

articles.title: Mapping a temporary food preparation area
articles.summary: Identify usable space and equipment when the usual kitchen layout is disrupted.

visual.alt: A compact shelves diagram labels Surface, Equipment, Clearance to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Identify a practical surface
paragraphs: List clean, stable areas already used for ordinary food preparation and note which are accessible to household members with different mobility needs.
A surface should not block exits, access to utilities or shared routes. Do not assume a bedroom, bathroom or other improvised area is suitable for preparing food.

sections.title: Match equipment to conditions
paragraphs: Record which ordinary utensils, lighting and storage locations are accessible without depending on unavailable appliances.
Do not improvise indoor use of outdoor stoves, barbecues or fuel-burning equipment. Combustion equipment can create serious fire and carbon monoxide hazards.

sections.title: Keep the plan limited
paragraphs: Use the map to find existing safe workspaces, not as an endorsement of unfamiliar cooking methods or food-storage conditions.
If water, refrigeration, ventilation or safe facilities are unavailable, consult appropriate current guidance rather than assuming that the temporary area can support every task.

articles.title: Writing household water-use priority notes
articles.summary: Help a household discuss competing needs without claiming a universal daily water allowance.

visual.alt: A compact checklist diagram labels Needs, Constraints, Contacts to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: List normal water dependencies
paragraphs: Discuss the activities that ordinarily depend on water, including drinking, food preparation, hygiene and any household-specific care or equipment needs.
Some needs may be time-sensitive or medically important. Do not replace individual professional advice with a generic household allocation.

sections.title: Note practical constraints
paragraphs: Record whether household members have difficulty carrying containers, reaching taps or accessing alternative facilities. Keep the note concise and avoid unnecessary sensitive personal details.
Identify which existing contacts or providers the household would consult about a supply interruption. Do not assume a planned alternative source is currently available or safe.

sections.title: Keep decisions adaptable
paragraphs: Review the notes when circumstances change and when the household receives reliable information about a particular interruption.
The guide deliberately gives no universal water quantities or purification instructions. Water safety and public-health decisions require appropriate reviewed advice.

articles.title: Keeping a neutral record of kitchen supply problems
articles.summary: Record food and water disruptions accurately for household follow-up.

visual.alt: A compact sequence diagram labels Observe, Record, Follow up to organise the nonhazardous household planning concepts in this guide.
visual.caption: Planning aid only; this diagram does not certify food or water safety.

sections.title: Capture observable facts
paragraphs: Write down the date, affected item or service, and what was directly observed, such as an absent delivery, damaged package or interrupted tap supply.
Distinguish observation from assumption. For example, a change in appearance is a reason to seek appropriate advice, not proof of a specific contamination cause.

sections.title: Avoid collecting unnecessary details
paragraphs: Keep the note focused on the practical household issue and the contact or reference number needed for follow-up, if any.
Do not copy full payment details, medical records or other sensitive identifiers into a general shared log. Photos may help with supplier disputes but should be stored privately.

sections.title: Record the outcome
paragraphs: Update the entry after a supplier response, replacement, inspection or other resolution. Mark unresolved items clearly so nobody mistakes a pending question for a completed check.
Do not treat an administrative log as evidence that food or water is safe. Escalate safety concerns through appropriate current official or professional channels.
